correctness.rationale: Two strong parts observe every core initially, leaving only private leaves to force. With one strong part, the only unobserved cores are its vacant pairs. Outside cores either face at least two vacant cores, or face one such core and their own unobserved leaf, unless an outside leaf was selected; the latter selection enables the necessary force when there is exactly one vacancy. Local observed cores are nonadjacent to the vacancies. For leaf-only sets, two vacancies in one part cannot be the first of those two cores forced; three or more in distinct parts prevent any first force. One vacancy has an observed core in another part; for two vacancies in different parts, an occupied pair remains in each part because the sizes are at least two, and each can force the other part's vacancy. The polynomial counts labeled pair states of weights 1,x,x,x²: subtract zero/one strong parts from the unrestricted term, then add the admitted leaf-only and one-strong configurations, including a nonempty outside leaf selection in the latter case with one vacancy. No singleton succeeds. Two-sets contribute E₂ across strong parts, 1+2+2(N−2) per size-two sole strong part, and four leaf-only choices only at N=4. Fresh direct adjacency and simultaneous-forcing enumeration checked 266,496 subsets over six profiles, including (2,6), (3,5) and (2,2,4) beyond the frozen test, with exact classifier and coefficient agreement. The finite replay is not the all-orders proof.

value.rationale: The result turns the known leaf-corona computation question into a closed all-cardinality evaluation for a natural infinite class with arbitrarily many unequal parts. Unlike a general sum over exponentially many candidate sets with a matching test, it uses polynomial products/powers in the part sizes and exposes the sharp minimum multiplicity. This is useful even after crediting known broad membership coverage and the pre-existing reliability transformation.
